extraction.name: SWE-Gym
extraction.description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents. It contains 2,438 real-world task instances sourced from 11 popular Python open-source repositories, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. The dataset also includes SWE-Gym Lite (230 easier, self-contained tasks) and SWE-Gym Raw (64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments spanning 358 repositories).
extraction.creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
extraction.citeAs: Pan, J., Wang, X., Neubig, G., Jaitly, N., Ji, H., Suhr, A., & Zhang, Y. (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Tasks were sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories from GitHub. The authors used SEART GitHub search to filter initial repositories, selecting Python repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories. They used SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert these repositories into task instances. They then semi-manually created executable environments for 11 selected repositories, configuring dependencies using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation. They used SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure gold patches pass more unit tests than original code.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world GitHub issues from 11 popular Python open-source repositories, including pandas, MONAI, moto, mypy, dvc, dask, modin, pydantic, conan, hydra, and bokeh. Each task includes a natural language description of the issue, a snapshot of the repository at the time the issue was created, and a set of unit tests.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Associated instances with version numbers (e.g., 1.2.3) using information from pyproject.toml, git tags, etc. Manually configured dependencies for each task instance. Used SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure gold patches pass more unit tests than original code. Filtered out failed instances. Required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours. Pre-built Docker images (6 TB) were released for reproducibility.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were performed by a subset of the authors, who manually configured dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. The gold patch (human-submitted code diff) was validated against unit tests to ensure correctness.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations are done by a subset of the authors
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench instance extraction script, SWE-Bench execution-based validation script, SWE-Bench versioning script (generalized to support versioning via script execution)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors publicly release SWE-Gym, models, and agent trajectories. Pre-built Docker images for each instance (6 TB) are released for reproducibility.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. Current models are research artifacts and not yet production-ready but could support critical open-source infrastructure. As agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require considerations around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate creation of malicious code.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas tasks comprising nearly one-third of the total while bokeh tasks represent only one percent. Repeated sampling shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, introducing a bias toward easier tasks when training on all successful trajectories. The dataset may also introduce distribution bias if environments are not carefully configured for specific codebase versions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11 with executable environments), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). Current SWE settings focus solely on task completion, neglecting human-in-the-loop collaboration which is essential for real-world software engineering. Tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those included in SWE-Bench, with more lines and files edited in gold patches. To avoid contamination, repositories used in SWE-Gym are separate from those used in SWE-Bench.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training language model based SWE agents using supervised fine-tuning and rejection sampling. Training verifier models (outcome-supervised reward models) for inference-time scaling. Use cases include training agents that can automatically resolve GitHub issues, self-improvement experiments, and research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.
